questions.problem: Suppose that a matrix $A$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=(\lambda +2)(\lambda -5)^{19},$ the rank of $(A-5I)^{5}$ equals $12,$ and the rank of $(A-5I)^{6}$ equals $9.$ If a basis of ${R}^{20}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $A$, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $6$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5?$
questions.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda =5,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $6$ is a vector $v$ such that 

$$
(A-5I)^{6}v=0\,\text{and}\,(A-5I)^{5}v\ne 0.
$$

Notice that $A$ must be a $20\times 20$ matrix.

- Since the rank of $(A-5I)^{5}$ equals $12,$ then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-5I)^{5}=20-12=8.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A-5I)^{5}v=0$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{5}$ of dimension $8$ in ${R}^{20}.$

- Since the rank of $(A-5I)^{6}$ equals $9,$  then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-5I)^{6}=20-9=11.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A-5I)^{6}v=0$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{6}$ of dimension $11$ in ${R}^{20}.$

Since $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{5}$ is a subspace of dimension $8$ in $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{6}$, which is a subspace of dimension $11,$ our basis can contain only $3$ vectors that lie in $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{6}$ but do not lie in $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{5}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(A-5I)^{6}-\text{nullity}(A-5I)^{5}=11-8=3
$$

 generalized eigenvectors of rank $6$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5.$

questions.problem: Suppose that a matrix $A$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -5)^{7},$ the nullity of $(A-5I)^{2}$ equals $1,$ and the nullity of $(A-5I)^{3}$ equals $2.$ If a basis of ${R}^{9}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $A$, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5?$
questions.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda =5,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ is a vector $v$ such that 

$$
(A-5I)^{3}v=0\,\text{and}\,(A-5I)^{2}v\ne 0.
$$

Notice the following:

- We are given that $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{2}$ has dimension $1.$ This means that the solutions to $(A-5I)^{2}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $1.$

- We are given that $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{3}$ has dimension $2.$ This means that the solutions to $(A-5I)^{3}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $2.$

Now, since $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{2}$ is a subspace of dimension $1$ in $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{3}$, which is a subspace of dimension $2,$ our basis can contain only $1$ vector that lies in $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{3}$ but does not lie in $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{2}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(A-5I)^{3}-\text{nullity}(A-5I)^{2}=2-1=1
$$

 generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5.$

questions.problem: Suppose that a matrix $B$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )={\lambda }^{4}(\lambda -\pi )^{5}(\lambda +3)^{2},$ the nullity of $(B-\pi I)^{2}$ equals $2,$ and the nullity of $(B-\pi I)^{3}$ equals $3.$ If a basis of ${R}^{11}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $B$, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\pi ?$
questions.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $B$ with eigenvalue $\lambda =\pi ,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ is a vector $v$ such that 

$$
(B-\pi I)^{3}v=0\,\text{and}\,(B-\pi I)^{2}v\ne 0.
$$

Notice the following:

- We are given that $\text{Null}(B-\pi I)^{2}$ has dimension $2.$ This means that the solutions to $(B-\pi I)^{2}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $2.$

- We are given that $\text{Null}(B-\pi I)^{3}$ has dimension $3.$ This means that the solutions to $(B-\pi I)^{3}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $3.$

Now, since $\text{Null}(B-\pi I)^{2}$ is a subspace of dimension $2$ in $\text{Null}(B-\pi I)^{3}$, which is a subspace of dimension $3,$ our basis can contain only $1$ vector that lies in $\text{Null}(B-\pi I)^{3}$ but does not lie in $\text{Null}(B-\pi I)^{2}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(B-\pi I)^{3}-\text{nullity}(B-\pi I)^{2}=3-2=1
$$

 generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\pi .$
